newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Trial opens in Vietnam's biggest fraud scandal.
newsitem.headline: Trial opens in Vietnam's biggest fraud scandal.

text.p: Vietnam's biggest corruption trial opened in Ho Chi Minh City on Thursday, with 20 defendants in the dock on charges of siphoning tens of millions of dollars from a company linked to the ruling Communist Party.
A showcase for the government's determination to punish graft, the trial is expected to end with a death sentence for the key defendants if they are found guilty.
The director of the Ho Chi Minh City-based trading firm, Tamexco, and a circle of his colleagues, relatives and friends stand accused along with state officials and senior bankers.
But the youth newspaper Thanh Nien, in a report delving into the murky details of how some $40 million vanished, said several other officials should be brought into the net for influence peddling.

"Financial links, such as receiving money for business trips abroad and buying cars, or using Tamexco money to waste money on big parties have been shown quite clearly," it said. "It is clear that those officials are related to the case."

Foreign journalists have not been allowed to cover the trial, which follows hard on the heels of another high-profile corruption trial on Tuesday which sent two people to the firing squad and several others to jail.
The tightly censored domestic press has been unusually frank about the latest case which puts Vietcombank, the country's biggest state-owned bank, in the spotlight.
Two of the bank's former director-generals and a former deputy are among the accused.
Dossiers compiled by the prosecution over more than a year of investigation were reported to have filled a minibus when they were taken to the Ho Chi Minh City People's Court.
A string of accusations has been levelled against Pham Huy Phuoc, director of the now-bankrupt import-export company.
He is alleged to have channelled cash from the company to his relatives and given his mistress gold worth more than $200,000 to buy a swanky villa in Ho Chi Minh City.
Local newspapers say he also had eight passenger vans for his own personal use and gambled away five of them in a card game.
The former Vietcombank officials are accused of illegally granting loans to Tamexco even when, as one report put it, Phuoc was "up to his ears in debt".
One of the central State Bank of Vietnam's deputy governors, Chu Van Nguyen, will give evidence at the trial, but he has not been named as a defendant.
In a country where war has been declared against rampant cronyism, bribery and secret deals, questions are now being asked about how the scandal was kept under wraps for so long.

Spurred by popular disgust with graft, the government is preparing new legislation to stamp out a scourge which has been fed by an environment of growing prosperity and continued state control in most sectors of the economy.
The draft of the new bill suggests that any state or military official found guilty of siphoning $27,000 or more should face a firing squad or at least be imprisoned for life.
The Tamexco case is expected to run until the end of the month.
